Strike found Ryujo only at 1606 at 06-30S 160-45E (after chasing a second sighting 75 mi NE of Ryujo), attack began 1620, i.e. about 91 min to find it. One SBD and one TBF turned back mechanical. Idea of striking Ryujo earlier was abandoned for fear planes 'would not be able to return before nightfall' (doctrine.md). 7 F4F stayed as CAP. Cv6 report: last plane launched 1708; at 1710 ordered to attack Ryujo, alternative landing at Guadalcanal.

column12: launched an attack group at about 1510, consisting of 31 SBD's armed with 1,000-pound bombs and 6 TBF's armed with torpedoes ... her striking group was launched on a hopeless mission

The convoy was sighted at 1040 'north of Guadalcanal 250 miles' (range from Guadalcanal, not from the carrier) and 'changed course to the northwest at about 1300', news that reached Saratoga about 0100 on the 24th. Planes flew on 'following instructions' to Henderson Field (all but one TBF) and spent the night there: 36 landed ashore. Why ashore: ONI says only 'following instructions'; inferred reason: the convoy was a search target far from the carrier and recovery on return was not expected (not stated). Next morning the group, minus two SBD forced back to the island field, rejoined Saratoga about 1130 (deferred rendezvous 0800 -> 1100).

ONI: 'Four were forced down', pilots and crews of three rescued, a fourth landed on Stewart Island. Cv6 report: 5 water landings out of fuel for the whole Enterprise air group that day (outcomes). Already in the database as a search_launch row; repeated here for the fuel-loss rows. Point option course 000 speed 10 kn (cv6 report).

Target report was false (code pad error, 'Yorktown scout' saw 2 CA + 2 CL); planes allowed to continue and met the real Shoho group north of Misima. Closing or not not stated. Lexington group landed by about 1345. No fuel losses recorded: 2 SBD shot down (one Lt Allen; one forced landing on Rossel Island, crew rescued).

Yorktown group recovered 1231-1300; one SBD crash landing wrecked. Enemy sighted by dive bombers 1032; attack 1058.

Heavy losses to fighters or fuel (outcomes); 7 TBDs came back so short of fuel they skipped recognition and were fired on by the Yorktown. Last plane landed about 1400.

column19: Japanese DUSK STRIKE launched knowing it would return after dark and with no fighter escort. 280 nmi is the flight leg ordered, not a measured distance to the target; the 200 nmi figure is the distance of TF 17 west of Takagi at 1747 (92 min after launch). Range_m left blank. 7 torpedo planes + 1 dive bomber shot down by CAP and 1 torpedo bomber crashed (as the page gives them). 18 survivors; all recovered by 2200 with searchlights, a few overflew TF 17 at about 1900. Losses on the night landing not stated on that page.

column12: At 09:15, the Japanese carriers launched a combined strike of 18 fighters, 33 dive bombers, and 18 torpedo planes ... [sighting] about 210 nmi apart
column19: The 210 nmi is the separation at 0822 when each side sighted the other, the page says both carrier forces then turned toward each other at high speed to shorten the return leg. Japanese strike therefore flew much less than 210 nm. Radius not stated. Lexington radar detected the strike at 68 nm (ONI).

column6: Japanese carriers (reported 2 CV at 320 deg 180 mi from Midway)
column12: The objective, enemy carriers, was calculated to be 155 miles distant, bearing 239 T. from this Task Force; one division of 10 VF ... with 35 VSB and 15 VTB ... Deferred departure was used
column19: 35 SBD (500 lb), 15 TBD, 10 F4F. RANGE AS STATED 155 mi (naval = nautical assumed), computed from an intercept course on a 140 deg 25 kn enemy; the enemy reversed course about 1 hour after launch and Hornet did not break radio silence. OPENING: wind light (4 kn) and directly away from the enemy, so every CAP relief and recovery lengthened the run back. Report uses 'zone plus 10' clock and writes the launch time as '090'; ONI shows 0700 (different zone, not converted). OUTCOMES: no Hornet fighter returned to the ship: they stayed with the SBD until forced to head for Midway for lack of gas; 5 pilots rescued (ONI: 8). 13 SBD of Bombing 8 landed at Midway for lack of gas, 2 in the lagoon out of gas; 11 gassed and returned to Hornet 1727. Scouting 8 and Bombing 8 never found the enemy. 15 TBDs (Waldron) found it and were lost to combat.

column12: By 0700 it was estimated that the Japanese carriers were about 155 miles distant on bearing 239 from the task force, and launching was begun ... Deferred departure was used, and the launching required about an hour
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-Midway/USN-CN-Midway-7.html (Our carrier attack on the enemy carriers, June 4)
column19: Agrees with the Hornet report. ONI: 'All the fighters exhausted their gasoline and landed in the sea before reaching Midway, but 8 pilots were rescued. All but 2 of the dive bombers eventually returned to the Hornet. Thirteen reached Midway, where 2 landed in the lagoon.' ONI adds the carriers turned away: 'Our carriers did not break radio silence'.

column12: launched 33 scout bombers, 14 torpedo planes and 10 fighters; carriers about 155 miles distant on bearing 239; Enterprise first group of 33 SBD launched 0906, torpedo group 0949 (cv6 report, zone +10)
column19: RANGE AS STATED (one estimate for Hornet and Enterprise). The Enterprise report (EM) gives clock times 0906 and 0949 on a zone +10 clock and the enemy position 'based on the 0810 contact report' as 30-05N 179-03W at 0930. McClusky's reverse-course search found the enemy at 1202 (report clock). Fighters lost the TBDs. Enterprise losses 4 June (cv6 report): 18 SBD, 10 TBD in the first phase and 1 F4F water landing 'out of gas; pilot recovered'; ONI: of the 33 SBD 18 failed to return, 'it is thought that most ... were forced down on the water when they ran out of fuel'.

column12: at about 0840 all the torpedo squadron (12 VTB), half the bomber squadron (17 VSB), and 6 fighters were launched ... To conserve fuel, the fighters were not launched till 0905
column19: NO RANGE STATED for Yorktown. PRACTICE: fighters held back 25 min to save fuel; bombers told to circle for 12 min before overtaking the slower TBDs. Yorktown's bombers returned and, ordered clear of the ship, 'two planes ... forced by lack of fuel to land on the water' (ONI ch.7).

column12: At 1730 an attack group of 24 SBD's ... was launched ... Position of enemy was given, as of 1900, as 31-40N 179-10W. At 1850 this force was sighted about 30 miles ahead
column19: NO RANGE STATED. 24 SBD (11 x 1,000 lb, 13 x 500 lb). 3 SBD shot down; all others landed 2034 after dark approach. No fuel loss. The Hornet report's range for her own launch is separate.

column12: At 1712, commenced launching the attack group, consisting of 26 VSBs ... At 2004, having failed to sight any major enemy force after conducting a 315-mile search, the attack group attacked an enemy CL or DD in a position 278 miles bearing 315 T. from the Hornet position at time of launching
column19: LONGEST STRIKE IN THE SET. 26 SBD. 278 miles is the target position AS STATED relative to the launch position (naval miles assumed nautical); 315 miles is the search distance flown. Outbound leg about 2 h 50 min (1712 to 2004). Night recovery: 'Most of the landings were made after complete darkness'; 'Few of the pilots had previous night carrier landing experience'; 'All planes returned with very little gas; one plane landed, out of fuel, in our arresting gear'; one landed in the water near Enterprise out of fuel, crew picked up in darkness by Aylwin. The intended target was believed 240 mi from Midway; Spruance's intent is in TF-16 report (not read).

column19: 265 miles is the distance flown outbound on 324 deg, NOT a distance to a target (range_m left blank); total searched was longer (then 33 mi on 230, then 150). Attacked a Katori-class cruiser at 2030. Night landings with 'many inexperienced pilots who had not qualified in night landings'; 'The performance of the entire group was excellent'. One SBD lost to AA; no fuel loss recorded; one Enterprise plane landed on Hornet.

column19: RANGE AS STATED, measured to the target as attacked from the 1015 position (nautical assumed). 1 SBD shot down by AA, rest recovered 1245. Enemy was retiring at about 28 kn.

column12: At 1245 an attack group was launched consisting of 31 SBD's ... 3 TBD ... and 12 VF ... Position of objective at 1350 ... course 270 speed 15 knots
column19: NO RANGE STATED. 'Our Group sustained no losses or damage.' The group departed 1315 and 'maneuvered to lose time' to let TBDs rendezvous (practice).

column12: 24 VSB were launched at 1530 ... The enemy force was at this time about 110 miles 264 T. from Hornet position
column19: RANGE AS STATED. Attack 1645; group returned without losses, recovered 1728.

column19: RANGE AS STATED for the carriers' reported position (naval miles taken as nautical). RETURN: Hornet was already dead in the water when the planes returned (1155) and they went to Enterprise. FUEL (see outcomes): 2 TBF water landings out of fuel and 1 TBF missing.

Returned to a crippled Hornet and landed on Enterprise: the 9 SBD all aboard by about 1330; of the TBF flight 'the remaining three made water landings after exhausting their fuel'.

Of the TBFs 4 survived the attack; 2 landed on Enterprise 1425, 2 ran out of gas over the force and made water landings.

column12: 2330 Helena radar contact bearing 315 T, distance 29,000 yards

column12: TBS: "This is CTF. Execute to follow: left to course 230."; thirty seconds later "From CTF: execute."

Nearly the same words in the DesRon 12 report (Cominch). Scarcely 10 minutes passed between the end of the countermarch and the opening of fire at 2346. Footnote 20: Halsey said that had the destroyers received radar contacts they would have passed on the opposite side from which the enemy were expected.

column12: At 2345 Helena requested permission over TBS to commence firing; misinterpreted as a request to acknowledge her last transmission (the radar contact on five ships); Scott answered "Roger"

Footnote 22 ONI: Scott said he had told the cruisers to open fire without his permission. DesRon 12 lessons: change the signal to commence firing or the way TBS messages are receipted.

column6: one of two heavy cruisers on the starboard bow, then a destroyer on the starboard quarter

column6: turn to starboard (right) away from the american column

Hough says the Fubuki and Furutaka were sunk or crippled and that Kinugasa and Hatsuyuki "withdrew".

column6: goto (mortally wounded) and the flag bridge

column14: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B5%E3%83%9C%E5%B3%B6%E6%B2%96%E6%B5%B7%E6%88%A6 ; section 青葉被弾 (cites Aoba Doesn't Sink pp.176-183; Otsuka p.170; Musashi vol.1)
column19: No time printed for this statement; the hour 23:46 was the researcher's conversion and has been removed. Japan time rows in this section begin 2145 = 2345; the article says the first hit came right after the first US salvo and four minutes later (2150 Japan time) Aoba was out of action. Combinedfleet: Aoba hit by up to forty 6-inch and 8-inch shells; bridge wrecked; No. 2 turret knocked out and No. 3 destroyed; four boilers out; Goto mortally wounded and 80 others killed. en-wiki: up to 40 shells.

column12: Furutaka, 1,500 m astern of Aoba, saw the gunfire of a dozen or more ships ahead at 2146:30 (Japan time); her captain ordered "left, battle torpedo action, right gun action"; she fired AA guns once, then turned right to place herself between Aoba and the enemy and opened fire at 2148
column14: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B5%E3%83%9C%E5%B3%B6%E6%B2%96%E6%B5%B7%E6%88%A6 ; section 古鷹被弾、沈没 (cites the Handy Edition photo book p.39 and others)
column19: No time printed for this statement; the hour 23:46 was the researcher's conversion and has been removed. Japan time; +2 h = 2346:30 and 2348. Furutaka fired 20 or 36 main rounds and 26 AA rounds per ja-wiki; Aoba saw her use a searchlight.

column12: The Japanese force was completely surprised
column19: Also Miller ("caught completely by surprise", printed p.146-147) and Hough ("caught the enemy by complete surprise", p.324-325). ONI Conclusions: surprise was the major factor; the enemy fired nothing for 7 minutes.

column12: while the US fleet had "eye" trouble the Japanese ships were completely blind
column19: Hough means no radar help; the sentence is about vision and radar together; not a statement about fitted equipment. See the fits rows.

column5: japanese force (as read in the Cominch commentary by San Francisco)
column12: No Japanese TBS or radio was heard; no enemy pyrotechnics or tactical signalling seen; an Amagiri-class destroyer at 1,100 yards did not appear to have a radar antenna; it is not known whether either enemy unit had radar; our force seems undetected until it opened fire

column19: Wartime; the Amagiri-class identification is the observer's. Also: no Japanese smoke screens; two cruisers first seen emerging from smoke from burning Japanese ships.

column12: Goto's force passed through rain squalls at 30 knots; at 23:30 the ships emerged from the last squall and began appearing on the scopes of Helena and Salt Lake City; the Japanese, whose warships were not equipped with radar, remained unaware of Scott's presence
column14: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Esperance ; section Battle, Prelude (cites Frank p.299; Cook pp.58-60; Morison pp.152-153)
column19: Wikipedia; books not seen.

column10: 4,800 yd, bearing 300 T (SF log); 4,600 yd to starboard (ONI)

column19: Cominch quotes the San Francisco log: about 2347, main and secondary on an unidentified enemy ship bearing 300 T, range 4,800 yd, "the left hand ship that had been located". Range 4,600 against 4,800. After a few salvos the target and another were on fire; fire shifted to an Amagiri-class destroyer approaching from the starboard beam (probably Fubuki per later accounts, not stated in these sources).

column6: a friendly-looking destroyer, probably Duncan, and an enemy cruiser and destroyer
column10: 2,000 yd forward of her starboard beam
column12: McCalla recorded sighting an apparently friendly destroyer 2,000 yards forward of her starboard beam; to the left of it an enemy cruiser and destroyer
column19: ONI: the friendly destroyer was probably the Duncan.

column12: just after San Francisco joined in the continuous fire to starboard Scott ordered "Cease firing" over TBS
column19: ONI footnote 24: McCalla's log has this TBS message at 2346, Salt Lake City's at 2347 (ONI judges 2347 more likely because TBS was busy with the "Roger" exchange). Cominch: 2347 Commander Task Group ordered cease firing because he thought the cruisers were firing at own destroyers, from their position and similar silhouettes; it "never did completely stop"; Boise and others kept firing on two burning ships. Cominch San Francisco log has the order at 2350, by voice as well as TBS. en-wiki 23:47. ja-wiki (Japan time 2147, citing Otsuka) says Scott feared the cruisers were firing on Duncan and the order was ignored by Helena and others.

column12: 2347 Commander Task Group ordered cease firing; he thought the cruisers were firing at own destroyers, because of position and similarity of silhouettes; Commander Destroyer Squadron TWELVE asked if his ships had been fired on and replied none so far as he knew
column19: See the ONI row for the time disagreement (2346 McCalla, 2347 Salt Lake City, 2350 San Francisco log).

column12: At 2347 Scott asked Capt. Tobin over TBS whether the destroyers had been fired upon; he replied none of his ships had as yet been fired on, and that he did not know on whom the cruisers were firing
column19: DesRon 12: about 30 seconds later he reported that own units were firing on him; fire of own units decreased but continued.

column12: A minute later the Farenholt was hit twice in the rigging, and Capt. Tobin reported the hits to the flagship
column19: Cominch DesRon 12 report has the hits on the fore yardarm and the top of No. 2 stack at 2350; fragments jammed the amidships torpedo mount; then one or more shells at the waterline on the port side near frames 65 and 85 which put the IC and plotting room out and disrupted power forward. ONI says two apparent 6-inch hits on the port side between 2353 and 2358. Whether Japanese or American shells hit her is not settled in the sources read (ONI and en-wiki say both).

column5: japanese targets of helena and boise (a cruiser, an unidentified ship, destroyers)
column12: US claim: Helena and Boise recorded that their three targets sank at about 2350; a minute later the destroyer engaged by San Francisco sank
column19: ONI: "In less than 5 minutes, Task Force SUGAR had apparently destroyed one heavy cruiser, one unidentified ship, and three destroyers"; later information (footnote 29) says only Furutaka, Fubuki and Natsugumo were certainly sunk. These first-phase "sinkings" were claims by the US ships; Aoba and Furutaka were damaged and Fubuki sank later (see below). The sources read do not say which of these the claims were.

column12: At about 2350 Boise's target disappeared from both radar screens, leaving her own splashes still showing; fire ceased after about 120 rounds; reports indicated the target was a destroyer which broke in two and sank
column19: The 5-inch AA battery's target at the centre of the van. ONI says Boise's main battery target was identified by several officers as a Nachi-class heavy cruiser, burning furiously before sinking, and that her 5-inch target, a destroyer, sank about the same time.

column12: By 2351, more certain of the location of the enemy vessels, Admiral Scott ordered the Task Force to commence firing
column19: Cominch (Boise's log): "Commence firing ordered by Commander Task Group, there being no doubt in his mind now about the presence of the enemy and the fact that own destroyers were clear." en-wiki 23:51 (cites Cook pp.70-77, Frank p.302, Morison pp.158-160). ja-wiki 2151 Japan time, after Scott ordered destroyers to flash identification lights. Cominch: at 2350 Scott had ordered recognition lights on, being unsure the destroyers had not been fired on.

column10: a destroyer which had turned about 90 degrees to starboard, range 2,600 yd
column12: San Francisco: after running parallel for about one or two minutes the destroyer turned away and was illuminated by searchlight; white bands round the forward stack and a lattice foremast showed it was Japanese; fire resumed once it had turned 90 degrees to starboard to 2,600 yd and gone to high speed; the second 8-inch salvo straddled; it burned, exploded, turned on its side and sank
column14: https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA637263/DTIC_ADA637263_djvu.txt ; Chapter XX, composite log (San Francisco log entry for 2351)
column19: The ship is described but not named in the report; ONI chronological outline has the destroyer closing to 1,400 yards on a parallel course at 2350 and sunk by both batteries at 2351. Parallel running at 1,400 yards with white-over-red lights and a blinker is "deception" per San Francisco's own commentary.

column12: At 2353 the Boise fired with both batteries using searchlights for illumination on an enemy cruiser, which retaliated; a minute later she received an 8-inch hit starting large fires near the captain's cabin; two or three 5.5-inch shells followed

Boise's searchlight use is put at 0009 by Cominch (4 hits at 0011-0012). ONI also has the 0009 searchlight and further hits at 0009 to 0013. So ONI has Boise hit at 2354-2355 and Cominch has none before 0010.

column12: US records give her as exploding and sinking at 2153 (Japan time)

The Japanese record in the same article puts the sinking 20 minutes later (see the 0013 rows).

column12: Until 2353 no enemy gun or torpedo fire had been encountered; our fire, concentrated into barely 7 minutes, apparently stopped them training guns; none of our ships had thus far used searchlights
column19: First hit on a US ship: ONI says Farenholt's two hits in the rigging at 2348 (probably by US or Japanese fire, not settled) and Boise at 2354; Cominch has nothing hit before about 0010, and says "up to this time none of our ships had been hit" at the 2400 entry. Cominch comment on the Japanese opening fire "about 20 minutes after action opened": San Francisco says it was so accurate that radar range might have contributed (San Francisco commentary).

column12: 2354 receives 8-inch hit; 2355 receives two or three 5.5-inch hits (ONI chronological outline, Boise column)

column6: japanese heavy cruiser (Kako class per Buchanan; Kinugasa class per Cominch)

column5: japanese destroyer (target of san francisco), "believed later sunk"
column12: 2356 DD now seen as enemy escapes to port (believed later sunk)
column19: Outline entry; flattened table, column assignment not marked.

column14: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Esperance ; section Battle, Action (cites Frank pp.302-304; Cook pp.73-79, 83-86; Dull p.228; Morison pp.160-162)

column12: three enemy destroyers were observed to form up and approach the rear ship of our formation at high speed in an endeavour to launch a torpedo attack, on a line of bearing

column12: at 2203 (Japan time) Kinugasa torpedoed the target she took for a "London-class" heavy cruiser; Boise saw the wake at 2206 and turned hard right, passing at 50 yards; Kinugasa fired 16 torpedoes in all, 80 main-gun and 11 AA rounds
column14: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B5%E3%83%9C%E5%B3%B6%E6%B2%96%E6%B5%B7%E6%88%A6 ; section 衣笠反撃と戦闘終了 (cites the Kinugasa war report and Otsuka)

column12: At 0006 a torpedo wake was observed to starboard; she came right with hard rudder and the torpedo passed about 50 yards astern

column12: At 0009 Boise, using searchlights to illuminate the target, reopened with both batteries on an unidentified ship to starboard, which promptly returned fire; she was simultaneously engaged by a heavy cruiser believed to belong to another enemy group
column19: Cominch log, 0009: target about 100 relative taken under fire with searchlight illumination; four known hits, two just above the second deck at frame 59 starboard at 0011 and two at frame 16 starboard at 0012; a heavy cruiser at about 045 relative made two known hits, one in the barbette of No. 1 turret at 0010 and one through the side into the 6-inch magazine between turrets 1 and 2 handling rooms at 0011. column10: barbette of No. 1 turret; side into the 6-inch magazine
column12: At 00:10 two shells from Kinugasa exploded in Boise's main ammunition magazine between turrets one and two; explosion killed almost 100 men; Boise veered out of the column
column14: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Esperance ; section Battle, Action (cites Frank pp.304-305; Cook pp.74-75, 88-105; Dull pp.228-229; Morison pp.162-165)
column19: Books not seen. Hits on Boise at 0010 are Cominch's time too. ONI: "A succession of 5-inch, 6-inch and 8-inch shells poured on the Boise for the better part of 4 minutes"; at 0013 "wrapped in flames, she fell out of the formation and retired to the southwest". ja-wiki (Japan time 2206 to 2213) says Kinugasa hit Boise with four 20.3 cm shells and that Boise turned left out of line at 2213 (0013).

column14: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B5%E3%83%9C%E5%B3%B6%E6%B2%96%E6%B5%B7%E6%88%A6 ; section 吹雪被弾、沈没 (cites Otsuka pp.170-171 and Aoba/Fubuki records)

column12: at 0013 she fell out of the formation and retired to the southwest; she had lost three officers and 104 enlisted men; two hours later, about 0305, she was rejoined
column19: Cominch: at 0305 the Boise was contacted making 20 knots. ONI (ch.7) says "Two hours later".

column12: At 0014 Salt Lake City received an 8-inch hit forward to starboard while manoeuvring to avoid Boise; at about 0015 another 8-inch hit to starboard with minor damage and a few casualties

column12: at 0016 the enemy cruiser could not withstand the concentrated fire and was seen to sink (US belief)

column10: to 330 T to close the enemy

column12: San Francisco ceases fire at 0020 after firing on a 3-stack cruiser, results unobserved

column12: Course was changed at 0027 to 220 T; the remainder of the Task Force then retired on course 205 T; McCalla designated to stay and help Boise

column19: Wikipedia. ja-wiki (Japan time): she lost way at 2240 (0040), the destroyer Hatsuyuki arrived at 0008 on the 12th (Japan time, 0208), crew ordered off at 0020 (0220) and she sank at 0028 (0228). Hough says she "limped away to sink later".

column12: At 0050 the Salt Lake City fired two star shells to illuminate the San Francisco, which was well ahead of the formation and whose friendly character was doubted; within 10 minutes they identified each other and SLC fell in behind the flagship

column10: passing west of the Russell Islands
column12: During the battle Jojima's group completed unloading at Guadalcanal and began its return unseen by Scott's warships, passing south of the Russells and New Georgia
column19: Hough says the Fubuki, Furutaka etc. engaged at about 2346 while the reinforcement group steamed outside the normal route. ONI says it is possible the Japanese took Scott's ships for the "one large and two small" seen by San Francisco's plane (ch.8, footnote 30). The group was near enough to Cape Esperance for Jojima's 2220 message to Goto; ja-wiki says its destroyers were later detached to help Furutaka and Kinugasa.

column12: at about 0100 Lt Cdr Taylor jumped from the starboard bridge shield, half an hour after giving the order to abandon the bridge; about 0200 Lt Kabat ordered all personnel to abandon ship

column19: Books cited by en-wiki not seen.
